questions.question: What does git add stage?
options: Every future change to a file
A snapshot of the selected working-tree content
Only files already committed
A remote branch
questions.explanation: git add copies the selected content into the index. Later edits must be staged again if you want them in the next commit.

questions.question: What does git switch -c feature create?
options: A remote repository named feature
A tag named feature
A copy of every remote branch
A new branch named feature and switches to it
questions.explanation: git switch -c creates a new branch at the chosen starting point (HEAD by default), then checks it out.

questions.question: What does git fetch normally do?
options: Overwrites working-tree files with remote files
Commits local changes
Merges every remote branch into the current branch
Downloads objects and updates remote-tracking references
questions.explanation: git fetch downloads repository data and updates remote-tracking references. It does not normally merge changes into your current branch.

questions.question: Which changes does git diff --staged display?
options: The working tree compared with the index
The index compared with HEAD
All commits on every remote branch
Only untracked files
questions.explanation: The staged diff previews changes currently prepared for the next commit. A plain git diff normally shows unstaged tracked changes.

questions.question: A tracked file has staged edits and further unstaged edits. What does plain git diff normally show?
options: Only the difference between the working tree and the index
Nothing until the file is committed
Only the difference between HEAD and the index
Both sets combined against the remote branch
questions.explanation: The index is the comparison baseline for a normal working-tree diff. Use --staged to inspect the already-staged part.

questions.question: What does this short-status line mean?
options: The file is staged for deletion only
The file is untracked
The file has both staged and unstaged modifications
The branch has two merge commits
questions.explanation: In short status, the first column describes the index and the second describes the working tree.

questions.question: Which command unstages config.yml while keeping its working-tree edits?
options: git clean -f config.yml
git reset --hard HEAD
git restore config.yml
git restore --staged config.yml
questions.explanation: --staged changes the index rather than discarding the working-tree edit. A normal restore without it targets working-tree content.

questions.question: What does this command normally discard?
options: Unstaged tracked changes in settings.ini, replacing them from the index
The entire Git repository
Every commit touching settings.ini
Only the remote version of settings.ini
questions.explanation: Without --staged or --source, restore normally copies the index version into the working tree for the selected path.

questions.question: What does git reset --soft HEAD~1 do on a branch with a parent commit?
options: Deletes all working-tree files
Moves the branch back one commit while leaving the index and working tree unchanged
Creates a new reversing commit
Moves HEAD but clears all staged changes
questions.explanation: A soft reset moves the branch reference but preserves staged and working-tree content. The former commit’s changes remain available to recommit.

questions.question: What does a mixed reset to HEAD normally do?
options: Deletes untracked files
Updates only remote-tracking branches
Resets the index to HEAD while preserving working-tree changes
Creates an annotated tag
questions.explanation: Mixed is the default reset mode. Resetting to HEAD commonly unstages changes without discarding their working-tree content.

questions.question: Which statement about git reset --hard is correct?
options: It is always safe for uncommitted work
It can discard tracked working-tree changes as well as reset the index
It only changes the commit message
It creates a backup branch automatically
questions.explanation: A hard reset aligns the index and tracked working tree with the target commit. Do not rely on reflog to recover edits that were never committed.

questions.question: A bad commit is already on a shared main branch. Which approach usually preserves existing history while undoing its change?
options: git revert <commit>
Edit the remote-tracking ref manually
git reset --hard <parent> followed by an unconditional force push
Delete the .git directory
questions.explanation: Revert records a new inverse change. It avoids rewriting the shared commits that collaborators may already have based work on.

questions.question: When is a fast-forward merge possible?
options: Whenever the two branches have the same name
Only when the working tree has untracked files
Only if both branches contain merge commits
When the current branch tip is an ancestor of the branch being merged
questions.explanation: A fast-forward simply moves the branch pointer along existing history. Diverged histories cannot be combined by only moving that pointer.

questions.question: What does --no-ff request when a fast-forward would otherwise be possible?
options: Create a merge commit instead of only moving the branch pointer
Refuse all merges
Delete the source branch automatically
Squash all repository history into one commit
questions.explanation: --no-ff preserves an explicit merge boundary. It does not itself squash commits or remove the merged branch.

questions.question: Why do replayed commits usually receive new object IDs during a rebase?
options: Rebase merely renames files alphabetically
Git assigns random IDs each time a commit is read
Their parent relationships and possibly other commit contents change
Only remote servers can preserve commit IDs
questions.explanation: A commit ID hashes the commit object, including its parent references. Replaying the same patch on another parent creates a different commit.

questions.question: After resolving a rebase conflict and staging the resolved file, what normally resumes the operation?
options: git fetch --continue
git switch --finish
git merge --start
git rebase --continue
questions.explanation: Staging marks the conflict resolution. --continue lets rebase proceed to the next commit in the replay sequence.

questions.question: You started a merge and want to abandon it. Which command is designed for that?
options: git branch --abort
git revert --all
git merge --accept-all
git merge --abort
questions.explanation: --abort attempts to restore the pre-merge state. Keeping unrelated uncommitted edits out of an operation makes recovery more predictable.

questions.question: During a normal merge into your current branch, which region is the current branch’s side?
options: The entire file is automatically staged
The lines after >>>>>>> only
The lines between <<<<<<< HEAD and =======
The text feature means the file is untracked
questions.explanation: In a normal merge conflict, the HEAD region is the current side. Resolve the intended content and remove the markers before staging.

questions.question: What does git stash push -u add compared with the usual tracked-change stash?
options: Untracked files
Every remote branch
The repository’s reflog history
Every ignored file regardless of flags
questions.explanation: -u includes untracked files. Ignored files require a different choice, such as --all, and may include local material you should handle carefully.

questions.question: A git stash pop encounters conflicts. What normally happens to the stash entry?
options: It is pushed to origin automatically
It is converted into a tag
It is retained so it can be handled after resolving the conflict
It is always deleted even if application fails
questions.explanation: pop drops the entry only after successful application. A conflicted application normally leaves the stash available.

questions.question: You add a tracked secrets.env file to .gitignore. What happens to its existing tracking?
options: It instantly disappears from remote history
Git deletes it from every commit
Git encrypts its previous contents
It remains tracked until explicitly removed from the index
questions.explanation: Ignore rules mainly affect untracked paths. Removing tracking also does not erase historical secrets; exposed credentials require separate remediation.

questions.question: What does this command do for an already-tracked local.env?
options: Erases every historical version
Deletes the working-tree file immediately
Renames it to .gitignore
Removes it from the index while leaving the working-tree file
questions.explanation: --cached targets the index. Commit the removal and add an appropriate ignore rule if the file should stay local.

questions.question: Your branch and its upstream have diverged. What does this command do?
options: Overwrites the remote branch
Refuses to integrate because a fast-forward is not possible
Rebases your branch automatically
Creates a merge commit anyway
questions.explanation: --ff-only prevents pull from introducing a merge commit or silently choosing a rebase when histories diverge.

questions.question: What is the purpose of -u here after a successful push?
options: Make feature a protected branch
Set origin/feature as the upstream for local feature
Remove the origin remote
Upload every local branch
questions.explanation: The upstream relationship supports default pull/push behavior and ahead/behind reporting. It is not repository access control.

questions.question: You made useful commits while HEAD was detached. What should you do to retain an easy branch reference to them?
options: Run git clean -fd
Create a branch at the current commit
Delete the index
Rename the .git folder
questions.explanation: A new branch keeps a named reference to the detached work. Otherwise it can become hard to find after switching away and eventually be garbage-collected.

questions.question: Which mechanism can help find a recent branch tip after a local reset?
options: The filesystem’s file extension database
The current .gitignore file
The reflog
The remote README rendered as HTML
questions.explanation: Reflogs record local reference movements. They are local, expire over time, and are not a universal backup of uncommitted file contents.

questions.question: What does git cherry-pick <commit> normally do?
options: Applies that commit’s change and records a new commit on the current branch
Merges every commit from the source branch
Creates a remote automatically
Moves the original branch pointer without changing files
questions.explanation: Cherry-picking selects a change for replay. The resulting commit usually has a different parent and therefore a different ID.

questions.question: Why does reverting a merge commit require choosing a mainline parent with -m?
options: Git needs the parent relative to which the merge change should be reversed
The flag supplies a replacement commit message
It chooses the remote authentication method
Merge commits contain no parent references
questions.explanation: A merge has multiple parents. The mainline selection defines the baseline for interpreting and reversing its changes.

questions.question: What distinguishes an annotated tag from a lightweight tag?
options: It is automatically pushed by every normal git push
It can only point to untracked files
It always moves automatically with the branch
It creates a tag object with metadata and a message
questions.explanation: Annotated tags carry metadata and can be signed. A lightweight tag is essentially a direct reference; tags do not move with branch development.

questions.question: What does origin/main normally represent in a local repository?
options: The current working directory
A local remote-tracking reference updated by fetch
A branch stored only on the remote and never locally
A live network connection that is always current
questions.explanation: Remote-tracking refs reflect the remote as last fetched. They can be stale until network synchronization occurs.

questions.question: Which commits does this log range select?
options: Commits common to both branches only
Every commit preceding the repository’s first commit
Commits reachable from feature but not from main
Only merge commits on main
questions.explanation: For revision traversal, A..B excludes commits reachable from A and includes those reachable from B.

questions.question: In git diff main...feature, what baseline is normally used?
options: The working tree compared with the index
The remote default branch regardless of main
The merge base of main and feature, compared with feature
Every commit on both branches printed as patches
questions.explanation: Three-dot diff is useful for the changes introduced on feature since its common ancestor with main. It differs from three-dot log traversal.

questions.question: What does git merge-base main feature identify?
options: A best common ancestor of the two histories
The branch with fewer commits
The newest untracked file
The repository’s configured username
questions.explanation: A merge base is an ancestry relationship used in merge and comparison operations. Criss-cross histories can have more than one best base.

questions.question: What does git bisect help locate?
options: A malformed SSH private key
The commit that introduced a reproducible regression
Every unused local branch simultaneously
A line that contains a syntax error without running tests
questions.explanation: Bisect searches a good-to-bad commit range using repeated test results. A reliable test and a correct starting range are important.

questions.question: What does git blame normally show for each line?
options: Which user last opened the file in an editor
Who originally designed the whole application
Only the author of the current branch
The commit that last changed that line in the selected history
questions.explanation: Blame attributes line changes to commits. It is an investigation aid, not proof of who caused a bug or who first conceived the code.

questions.question: What is a useful purpose of git worktree add?
options: Check out another branch into a separate working directory sharing the repository
Automatically deploy the branch to production
Duplicate every object into an unrelated repository
Make all branches share one index
questions.explanation: Linked worktrees enable parallel working directories with separate checkouts. Git normally prevents checking out the same branch in multiple worktrees simultaneously.

questions.question: What does --recurse-submodules request during a clone?
options: Flatten every submodule’s history into the parent
Initialize and clone the configured submodules as well
Ignore .gitmodules
Replace all submodules with symbolic links
questions.explanation: Submodules refer to other repositories at recorded commits. Recursive cloning populates their working directories instead of leaving only the parent checkout.

questions.question: Why run this command before a destructive clean?
options: It commits untracked files to a backup branch
It previews untracked files and directories that would be removed
It verifies that all tests pass
It permanently deletes ignored files too
questions.explanation: -n is a dry run and -d includes untracked directories. Actual clean removal can destroy work that Git has never stored.

questions.question: What protection does --force-with-lease provide compared with an unconditional force push?
options: It encrypts the pushed commits
It prevents all possible accidental overwrites
It checks that the remote ref has an expected value before replacing it
It locks the branch forever
questions.explanation: A lease protects against unexpected remote updates. Its default expectation can be affected by fetched remote-tracking refs, so it is not a universal safety guarantee.

questions.question: Why should you be cautious amending a commit already shared with others?
options: The amended commit has a new ID and may require history rewriting to publish
Amend always deletes all previous commits
The command only works on remote branches
It makes the commit impossible to review
questions.explanation: Amend creates a replacement for the current tip commit. Collaborators may already depend on the old ID.

questions.question: After staging a file, you edit it again and run plain git commit. Which version is normally committed?
options: All working-tree edits whether staged or not
Only the file version on origin
The staged snapshot, not the later unstaged edits
An empty version of the file
questions.explanation: A normal commit records the index. Stage subsequent edits if they should also be included.

questions.question: What does this path-limited reset do?
options: Deletes config.yml from all history
Resets config.yml in the index to HEAD without moving the branch
Discards the working-tree copy unconditionally
Moves the branch to a commit named config.yml
questions.explanation: The path form resets index entries. It is different from resetting the branch tip to another commit.

questions.question: What does this restore command normally change?
options: The remote branch named app.py
The working-tree copy of app.py using the version in v1.0
Every file in the repository
The current branch to point at v1.0
questions.explanation: --source chooses the content source. Without --staged, the destination is normally the working tree for the specified path.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of sparse checkout?
options: Limit which tracked paths are populated in the working tree
Automatically split a repository into submodules
Remove unwanted history from the remote
Encrypt selected directories
questions.explanation: Sparse checkout narrows the working-tree view. It does not by itself remove historical objects or change repository access permissions.

questions.question: For an ordinary non-merge tip commit, what does HEAD~1 refer to?
options: Its first parent
The upstream remote branch
The next commit that will be created
The first commit in the repository
questions.explanation: The ~ operator follows first-parent ancestry. ~1 is one first-parent step backward.

questions.question: For a merge commit, what does HEAD^2 select?
options: The second file changed in the merge
Its first parent’s first parent
The second-most-recent remote branch
Its second parent
questions.explanation: ^n selects a numbered parent. ~n instead walks first-parent ancestry repeatedly.

questions.question: What is a suitable purpose for a .gitattributes rule with text and eol settings?
options: Configure branch protection on GitHub
Change every file’s executable permission
Control text normalization and checkout line-ending behavior
Store repository passwords securely
questions.explanation: Attributes can describe path-specific content handling. They are distinct from ignore rules and hosting-service branch policies.

questions.question: What does git rerere help reuse?
options: Recorded conflict resolutions for similar future conflicts
Every commit message from a different repository
Remote authentication tokens
The operating system’s file cache
questions.explanation: rerere records how conflicts were resolved and can reapply matching resolutions later. Review the result rather than assuming every reused resolution is appropriate.

questions.question: During a normal merge into main, what does git checkout --ours -- config.yml choose for that conflicted path?
options: The version from the remote default branch automatically
The incoming branch’s version
A merged version containing both sides
The current main-side version
questions.explanation: In a normal merge, ours refers to the current side. Stage the file afterward if that selection is the intended resolution.

questions.question: Are executable client-side hooks in .git/hooks automatically distributed by a normal clone?
options: Only if the repository has a README
Only if the branch is called main
No; hook installation requires a separate arrangement
Yes, every hook is part of every commit
questions.explanation: The local .git directory is not tracked as project content. Teams can version hook scripts elsewhere and arrange installation explicitly.
